---
title: "Coverage of R itself"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, comment = "#>")
```

covr can measure the coverage of R itself: the R code of base and the other packages that ship with R, and the C, C++ and Fortran code of the R executable, its shared libraries and the compiled code of those packages.
The coverage comes from running R's own test suite, `make check-all`.

## Who this is for

This is for people who build R, such as R core and the maintainers of the continuous integration (CI) of the [r-svn](https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn) mirror, and for developers who want to know what R's tests do and do not exercise.
It is not for measuring the coverage of your own package, see `package_coverage()` for that.

A ready-made GitHub Actions workflow lives in [r-devel/actions](https://github.com/r-devel/actions).
That workflow is the maintained version of what is described here, so use it rather than copying the commands below.
This article explains what it does and why.

## How it works

R code and compiled code are measured differently.

* **R code.** `instrument_base_r()` rewrites the lazy-load databases of the base packages so that every function counts the expressions it evaluates, and adds a hook to the base package loader.
  The hook makes every R process that loads base, including the many R processes that the tests start, count the code it runs and write its counts to the directory in the `COVERAGE_DIR` environment variable when it exits.
  `base_r_code_coverage()` then combines all the traces.
* **C, C++ and Fortran code.** R is compiled with gcov instrumentation (`--coverage`), so the programs write `.gcda` files as they run.
  `base_r_compiled_coverage()` runs gcov on the build directory and maps the results to the source files.

Both return an ordinary covr coverage object, so `lcov()`, `percent_coverage()`, `report()` and the other functions work on them.

## Requirements

* A Unix-like system with the tools to build R, `gcc` and `gcov`, and, for the tests that need a display, `xvfb-run`.
* The R sources, for example a checkout of r-svn.
* A second, normally optimized, build of R from the same sources, with covr and its dependencies installed in a separate library.
  Instrumenting needs to byte-compile all of base, which is about ten times slower in the unoptimized gcov build (19 minutes instead of 2).
  The byte code does not depend on the compiler flags, so the fast R can instrument the library of the gcov build.
* covr must stay installed at the same path as long as R is instrumented, because the path of its `covr.so` is baked into the loader of base.
* Optionally `genhtml` from lcov for an HTML report.

## Workflow

The commands use these variables, exported so that the R code below can read them.

```sh
export SRC=$HOME/r-svn                  # R sources
export BUILD=$HOME/build/gcov           # R with gcov instrumentation
export BUILD_FAST=$HOME/build/fast      # R at normal optimization, only runs covr
export COVR_LIB=$HOME/build/covr-lib    # covr and its dependencies, installed by BUILD_FAST
export TRACES=$HOME/build/traces        # where the R processes write their counts
```

### 1. Build R with gcov

Keep the source references of the packages, which the line numbers of the coverage come from, and turn off optimization so that the line counts make sense.
Use the same configure options as the regular build, here those of the r-svn Linux job, and build with the recommended packages.

```sh
export R_KEEP_PKG_SOURCE=yes
FLAGS='-g -O0 --coverage'
mkdir -p $BUILD && cd $BUILD
$SRC/configure --enable-R-shlib --with-blas --with-lapack --disable-java \
  CFLAGS="$FLAGS" CXXFLAGS="$FLAGS" FFLAGS="$FLAGS" FCFLAGS="$FLAGS" \
  LDFLAGS=--coverage
make -j$(nproc)
```

### 2. Build a fast R and install covr

```sh
mkdir -p $BUILD_FAST $COVR_LIB && cd $BUILD_FAST
$SRC/configure --enable-R-shlib --with-blas --with-lapack --disable-java \
  --without-recommended-packages
make -j$(nproc)
R_LIBS=$COVR_LIB bin/Rscript -e 'install.packages("covr", lib = Sys.getenv("R_LIBS"))'
```

### 3. Instrument

Run this with the fast R, pointing it at the library of the gcov build.

```sh
R_LIBS=$COVR_LIB $BUILD_FAST/bin/Rscript -e '
  covr::instrument_base_r(
    Sys.getenv("SRC"),
    lib = file.path(Sys.getenv("BUILD"), "library"),
    trace_dir = Sys.getenv("TRACES")
  )'
```

Delete the `.gcda` files afterwards so that building and instrumenting do not count.

```sh
find $BUILD -name '*.gcda' -delete
```

### 4. Run the checks

Set `COVERAGE_DIR` to the trace directory for all the processes the tests start.
Use `make -k` so that one failing test does not stop the others, and do not fail the job on test failures, because the coverage is still useful.
Setting `TEST_MC_CORES` runs some of the tests in parallel.

```sh
mkdir -p $TRACES && cd $BUILD
COVERAGE_DIR=$TRACES xvfb-run -a make -k check-all || true
```

### 5. Collect and report

Collect the coverage with the fast R, before calling `uninstrument_base_r()`, which deletes the counter file.
The paths in the files are relative to the sources, such as `src/main/eval.c`, which is what Codecov needs to match them to the repository.

```sh
R_LIBS=$COVR_LIB $BUILD_FAST/bin/Rscript -e '
  src <- Sys.getenv("SRC")
  r <- covr::base_r_code_coverage(Sys.getenv("TRACES"), src)
  c <- covr::base_r_compiled_coverage(Sys.getenv("BUILD"), src)
  covr::lcov(r, "lcov-r.info")
  covr::lcov(c, "lcov-c.info")
  covr::percent_coverage(c(r, c))'
```

Upload the two files to Codecov with the flags `r` and `c`, for example with `codecov/codecov-action`, so that the coverage of the R and compiled code are reported separately.
To get an HTML report, run `genhtml --ignore-errors source -o html lcov-r.info lcov-c.info` in `$SRC`.

When you are done, `uninstrument_base_r()` restores the library of the gcov build.

## Pitfalls

* Collect before `uninstrument_base_r()`, which deletes the counter file.
* Do not move or reinstall covr while R is instrumented.
* Instrument with a fast R, not with the gcov build itself.
* Remove the `.gcda` files after instrumenting and before the checks.
* Build with `R_KEEP_PKG_SOURCE=yes`, otherwise there are no line numbers for the R code.
* Do not fail the job when the checks fail.

## What is not instrumented

Some code is deliberately not instrumented, and does not show up in the coverage at all, not even as code that never ran.

* The functions in `base_r_exclusions()`, whose code R's own checks inspect: `pbinom()`, `simplify2array()`, `rematchDefinition()`, the functions the compiler inlines (`compiler:::safeBaseInternals`) and the internal generics of base (`.internalGenerics`).
  Pass your own list to the `exclusions` argument of `instrument_base_r()` to change this, e.g. add to `base_r_exclusions()` or use `NULL` to instrument everything, which makes some checks fail.
* Functions whose body is a constant or a call to `UseMethod()`, which have no code to cover.
* Default arguments of functions, which `R CMD check` compares with the documentation.
* Functions of base whose installed code differs from its source files, e.g. as they were created by other code, as they have no source references.

`instrument_base_r()` returns the functions it left out (`excluded`, by package) and the functions of base without source references (`no_srcref`), so a CI job can print them:

```r
info <- covr::instrument_base_r(src, lib = lib, trace_dir = traces)
str(info$excluded)
info$no_srcref
```

## Expected warnings

The checks report a few warnings with an instrumented R, which you can ignore.

* In base, "undocumented code objects" for the bindings starting with `.covr`.
* `abort` in compiled code, from libgcov.
* `__sprintf_chk` in compiled code, from the toolchain.

## Typical numbers

On 8 cores with R-devel r90937, with no test failures:

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| Build | 18 min |
| Instrument | 2 min |
| `make check-all` | 58 min |
| Collect | 50 s |

| Code | Coverage |
|---|---|
| R | 67.3% |
| C and C++ | 75.3% |
| Fortran | 71.8% |
| Total | 72.3% |

## Reference

* `instrument_base_r()` and `uninstrument_base_r()` instrument and restore the base packages.
* `base_r_code_coverage()` collects the coverage of the R code.
* `base_r_compiled_coverage()` collects the coverage of the compiled code.
